The biggest red flag is the premise itself. The blog argues that if someone steals your password, they 'know you' and can 'build a fake account.' That is a massive, absolute overstatement of the threat. If someone steals a password, they have stolen a key to your digital door. That doesn't mean they have the master key to your house, your bank account, or your identity. It just means they can walk in.

The article also suggests that 'remember me' is just a username and password, which is technically true for a password-protected account, but it completely ignores the reality of modern authentication systems. Even if someone steals your password, they might not have your 'remember me' enabled, or they might not have access to your email, your bank, or your social media. The blog treats a password like a magic wand that gives someone unlimited power, which isn't how these systems work.

The part about 'hacking' is the one that actually holds up. The article mentions that hackers use 'in-game accounts' to steal data. That is exactly right

I remember that story about the two college students in the 1980s. They took a student loan and a credit card, opened new accounts in the student's name, and paid the payments off by 2002. The credit bureaus didn't catch it until the students started paying off the accounts in 2004. The loan company called it a "card sketching" scheme.

The banks had actually warned them about the fraud risk when they were setting up the accounts, but the students just ignored the warnings. Even though the bank couldn't see the fraud, it was a huge risk for the bank because they were paying out to accounts that weren't actually theirs. The students' parents, who were the ones who put the money in, had no idea the banks had been involved.

When the banks finally called the students, the kids told them they were going to be in trouble. The bank said they would write off the debt, but the students said they would get a letter about the student loan they had taken out. The students argued that the bank could have foreclosed on the accounts if they had known the debt was actually coming from a student. They argued that the bank was in the best position to foreclose if they had known.

It's a good reminder of how easy it is for someone to set up their own identity in a bank's name without the bank noticing.
